newsitem.title: USA: Tame wages to balance rising US labor costs in Q2.
newsitem.headline: Tame wages to balance rising US labor costs in Q2.

text.p: Restrained wage gains are expected to verify that U.S. employment costs were relatively benign last quarter, despite a slight increase predicted for total compensation, economists said.

According to a Reuters survey, economists predicted the Labor Department's Employment Cost Index (ECI), due Tuesday at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT, will show labor expenses overall rose 0.8 percent in the second quarter. That follows a mild 0.6 percent gain in the January-to-March period.
But the main component in the compensation package, wages and salaries, probably rose at a more sober pace.

Marilyn Schaja, money market economist at Donaldson, Lufkin and Jenrette Securities Corp, forecast that wages and salaries rose 0.7 percent. "In the first quarter, wages were up 0.9 percent, so this is actually a better mix," she said.
The tame 0.3-percent increase in average hourly earnings embedded in the June employment report foreshadowed a smallish increase in the wages number, experts said.
"Using the weights per industry for employment actually reduces the wage gains even more for the second quarter," said Brian Fabbri, chief economist at Paribas Corp.
"In other words, people who got jobs in the second quarter were lower wage earners than in the first quarter," he added.
Given the long period of steady labor costs, analysts said the bond market would probably be sensitive to even a one-tenth of a percentage point variance from the consensus forecast.
Volatility in the series is unusual because it encompasses such a large aggregate of compensation, they said.

A 0.7-percent reading will probably add to the already constructive tone of the market, while a higher number was seen sparking worries that the dreaded cycle of overpaying amidst a shortage of job-seekers was finally underway.

On a year-over-year basis, the Employment Cost Index was expected to extend, by at least another quarter, the string of sub-3.0 percent increases that has been in place since early 1995, economists said.
The expected quarter-to-quarter increase would translate into about 2.8 percent in the 12 months since June 1996.

"I don't think this will continue over the course of the year, especially if benefits pick up," said Jonathan Basile, an economist at HSBC Markets Inc. "They have been probably the largest contributor to keeping the ECI under 3.0 percent.

Basile said medical care services, a useful indicator of benefit costs, rose about 0.8 percent in the second quarter, with anecdotal reports showing that Health Maintenance Organization (HMO) premiums are going to rise for the year.
Employers laid out just 0.1 percent more for benefits in the first quarter than in the final period of 1996, Labor Department data showed.
